questions.q: List the six major supporting characters in "One Centimetre" and state the single dominant narrative function each serves (e.g., foil, antagonist, catalyst, mentor, institutional voice, truth-revealer).
questions.a: Correct answer: Xiao Ye (moral compass/foil → later site of betrayal), Bus Conductor 1 (arbitrary rule enforcer), Temple Guard (petty bureaucratic antagonist), Old Woman with Scales (truth-revealer of societal deception), The Writer (mentor in rhetorical strategy), Temple Officials (institutional voice offering hollow restitution). A wrong answer that merely lists names without functions reveals the student sees characters as plot points rather than structural elements — a Class 10-level comprehension error that fails Class 12 analytical demands.

questions.q: Explain in your own words how Xiao Ye's role SHIFTS from the bus scene (where he demands a ticket) to the temple scene (where he is measured) to the final measurement at home. What does this progression reveal about the story's view of childhood innocence?
questions.a: Correct answer: On the bus, Xiao Ye enforces ritual honesty ("You don't keep your word!"), embodying childhood's rigid moral clarity. At the temple, he becomes a passive victim of institutional power — measured, humiliated, silenced. At home, he refuses measurement ("I don't trust you!"), showing innocence corrupted into suspicion. This trajectory reveals childhood innocence not as static purity but as a fragile construct dismantled by adult hypocrisy and institutional arbitrariness. A wrong answer describing only plot sequence misses the thematic arc — the student is summarizing, not analyzing character as thematic vehicle.

questions.q: The temple guard says: "The International Standard Ruler is in Paris, made of pure platinum. Did you know that?" Apply the concept of 'institutional gaslighting' to analyze how this statement functions as a power move. What specific psychological effect does it have on Tao Ying?
questions.a: Correct answer: The guard invokes an inaccessible, unimpeachable authority (Paris, platinum, international standard) to invalidate Tao Ying's lived reality. This is institutional gaslighting: replacing empirical evidence (the boy's height yesterday) with an abstract, unverifiable standard. The psychological effect: Tao Ying is "flummoxed" — her confidence collapses not because she's wrong, but because the system controls the definition of truth. A wrong answer focusing only on the guard's rudeness misses the structural violence — the student hasn't grasped how supporting characters embody systemic oppression.

questions.q: Compare the old woman's 'flattering scales' and the Writer's advice to "open with a strong and righteous claim, fawned by a passage of stunning originality." Both characters mediate truth. Analyze the difference in their ethical stance toward deception.
questions.a: Correct answer: The old woman's scales deliberately falsify reality for comfort ("make people seem lighter... taller") — a consensual deception society accepts ("fitness scales"). The Writer teaches Tao Ying to weaponize rhetorical deception ("grieving soldiers always win") to extract justice from an unjust system. The old woman enables self-delusion; the Writer enables strategic resistance. Both reveal truth as negotiable, but the old woman's deception soothes while the Writer's empowers. A wrong answer calling both "liars" flattens the moral complexity — the student hasn't distinguished between complicit and resistive deception.

questions.q: Evaluate the temple officials' offer of money and tickets as 'restitution.' Is it genuine justice or institutional damage control? Defend your judgment using evidence from Tao Ying's rejection and her final request ("explain to my son... that his mother has not done anything wrong").
questions.a: Correct answer: It is damage control, not justice. The officials arrive "prepared" with money after verifying the wall-mark was inaccurate — they protect the institution, not the victim. They offer transactional compensation (money/tickets) for a moral injury (public humiliation, broken trust). Tao Ying rejects both because "that day's happiness can never be bought again." Her demand — an explanation to her son — seeks restorative, not retributive, justice: restoring the child's faith in his mother's integrity. A wrong answer accepting the offer as "fair" reveals inability to distinguish procedural closure from moral repair — a critical gap for board exam 'critical thinking' questions.

questions.q: Write a 150-word monologue from the perspective of the temple guard (youth in red) the night after the incident, revealing his internal justification for his actions. Use textual details (his nervousness, his "edict from on high" posture, his fear of the crowd) to make it psychologically plausible.
questions.a: Expected criteria: Monologue must (1) use first-person voice, (2) incorporate at least three textual details (e.g., "earthworm" mark, crowd pressure, "International Standard Ruler" bluff, Tao Ying's calm confidence), (3) show the guard's insecurity beneath authoritarian performance, (4) avoid cartoonish villainy — he believes he's doing his job. A poor answer makes him purely evil or purely sympathetic without tension; this reveals the student cannot inhabit a character's limited perspective — a failure of the 'empathetic imagination' skill required for Class 12 creative response questions.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Supporting characters are secondary figures in a narrative who interact with the protagonist to advance the plot, reveal the protagonist's traits through contrast or parallel, embody thematic ideas, and represent societal forces or ______.
Fill in the blank: Imagine you're watching a play where the main actor (Tao Ying) is surrounded by a chorus of voices — some mocking, some helping, some ______ destroying her carefully built world.
What is Supporting characters? State the definition given in this lesson.
questions.a: Supporting characters are secondary figures in a narrative who interact with the protagonist to advance the plot, reveal the protagonist's traits through contrast or parallel, embody thematic ideas, and represent societal forces or institutions.

questions.q: What common mix-up does this lesson flag about Supporting characters?
questions.a: Students treat supporting characters as 'minor' and therefore less important for exams.

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student must be able to: (1) identify each supporting character's narrative function (foil, catalyst, thematic symbol, institutional representative), (2) trace how each character's interaction with Tao Ying reveals her evolving psychological state, and (3) write a structured PEEL-paragraph analysis linking a supporting character to a.
